content.thinking:
I'm thinking through the design of a koala gripping a eucalyptus branch mounted on a stand, sizing it realistically at around 0.6-0.7 meters tall in a sitting, hugging pose, with a base plinth supporting the branch.

I'm working out the pose so the face isn't hidden behind the trunk—trying a horizontal branch running left-right instead, with the koala sitting on top facing forward and gripping the branch with its hands.

Settling on a composition: a wooden plinth base with a thick eucalyptus trunk rising and tilting slightly, the koala seated upright astride a sloping branch so the pose stays clean and recognizable from the front.

Let me rethink the tree structure more concretely: a main trunk leaning slightly with a tapered radius, and a stout horizontal branch stub sprouting forward near the top where the koala's rump can rest, so it reads as sitting in a fork rather than hugging the trunk head-on.

I'm simplifying this to a single horizontal branch running along the X-axis in front at chest height that acts as the main support, with both arms reaching forward to grip it rather than trying to make an asymmetrical pose work.

Actually, I think the more natural solution is a branch running along the Z-axis at a slight upward slope, with the koala sitting astride it mid-length, rump resting on the branch, torso upright, and arms draping forward around it the way real koalas rest on branches.

The branch continues forward into leafy twigs near the face for nibbling and extends backward into another leafy end, with hind feet gripping the branch on either side below. For the stand, I'm picturing a forked trunk rising from a plinth, splitting into two branches — one leafy one trailing back, and the main one angling forward where the koala sits — and now I'm working out the plinth's dimensions and position.

For the skeleton rig, I want the root joint to be the hips, with the stand parts attached rigidly to that same joint so everything moves together only when the hips themselves move, keeping the whole structure simple and stable at roughly 1.35 meters tall including the leaves.

Settling on `stand` as the root with the spine chain branching from hips. Now I'm working out the branch geometry—placing the trunk and curved sitting branch using a catmull spline, positioning the koala at the midpoint with the plinth and trunk coordinates set up in 3D space.

Thinking through koala proportions: sitting height from branch to ear tops around 0.62m, giving a total figure height near 1.25m plus leaf sprigs, with a pear-shaped torso roughly 0.30m across the hips that needs a branch thick enough for the arms to wrap around comfortably.

Now I'm working out arm placement, positioning shoulders and hands so the limbs reach forward and down to grip the branch with realistic length, then building the hands with palm boxes, finger sweeps, and curled opposable thumbs to grip around it.

I'm defining the branch's centerline as a series of points curving from the base up through the seat area to the tip, with tapering radius from thicker at the base to thinner near the tip.

Now I'm placing the koala at the seat with its rump resting slightly into the branch for contact, and adding a second branch that sprouts behind it as a vertical trunk the koala leans against — running up to about y=1.25 with leafy sprigs at the top, forming a Y-shaped structure overall.

For the body, I'm laying out the spine chain from hips through chest and neck to the head, giving it the pear-shaped seated posture typical of a koala, and checking the proportions against a roughly 60cm sitting height to make sure the head and ear placement feel right relative to the seat height.

So sit height comes to roughly 0.64m, with the overall model reaching up to about 1.4-1.45 with leaf clusters, and a plinth base from 0 to 0.07. Now I'm thinking through the koala's body anatomy, starting with sweeping the spine from hips to neck with a varying radius profile.

For the elliptical cross-section I'm defining radius half-extents along width and depth, with hips wider at 0.17 and chest narrower at 0.14, plus a forward belly shift to capture the seated posture with a rounded bottom. I'm working out the sweep frame orientation and normal directions, deciding to keep the spine curve simple without additional shifting for now, then moving on to laying out the joint chains starting with the spine.

Now I'm defining the full skeleton: a spine chain running hips-spine2-chest, a neck chain into head/jaw/ear joints, then separate arm chains down to shoulders-elbows-wrists-hands with finger sub-chains, and hind leg chains from hip-knee-ankle-foot. I'm positioning the hind legs so the koala sits astride the branch with knees splayed outward and feet wrapping around the sides of the branch near its surface, working out approximate coordinates for hip, knee, and foot joints relative to the branch's height and radius.

Simplifying the feet to flat paw boxes at the branch sides with curled toes, keeping the koala's fused-toe grouping in mind.

I should get a thorough first draft done, preview the render, and iterate on exact positioning afterward rather than perfecting coordinates now. For texture, I'm planning to use cell-based fur painting with a small size setting.

Writing fur color ramp logic...

For the ear, I'll build it as two extruded discs—a larger gray outer disc and a smaller cream inner disc sitting slightly proud, with white fur tufts along the rim. For the nose, I'm going with a dark box shape with a pixel-art texture mapped on, giving it glossy highlights and nostril details on the front face.

For the head, I'm reconsidering the pure box approach since it reads too Minecraft-ish; instead I'll compose it from a main skull box with a painted face (eyes, brow, cheek fur, muzzle) plus separate nose, cheek fluff, and ear pieces, keeping everything on a consistent texel grid—0.02 for the body, finer scales like 0.015 or 0.01 for smaller details like the eyes, to keep that chunky pixel-art look while still having enough resolution on the head.

I'll settle on halving the texel for head details relative to the body (0.01 vs 0.02) rather than an awkward in-between size, since mixing arbitrary densities looks inconsistent. Checking the math: at this texel size and roughly 3m² of total painted surface area including bark and plinth, a 1024-texel paint sheet gives enough resolution—around 10 texels per 0.02m unit—so the body painting should hold up fine.

I'm reconsidering whether 1024 is enough or if I should bump the atlas up to 4096, but I'll start conservative and check actual texel counts before scaling up; plinth tile textures also share the atlas budget alongside the paint sheet. For the head shape, a boxy pixel-art style head paired with smooth rounded sweep-based body tubes could clash visually, so I'm weighing whether to reduce the sweep sides (like 8-sided, flat-shaded) to keep the whole model's silhouette consistently blocky and voxel-like rather than mixing smooth curves with sharp pixel cells.

I'm leaning toward faceted 8-sided limbs with slightly smoother 10-12-sided bodies, treating hard-edged texels as a separate requirement from faceting since they don't need to match. Now I'm sketching the full parts list, starting with the stand: a tiled wood-plank plinth, a darker beveled base slab, brass corner plates, screws, and a small engraved front plaque where I'll need to hand-draw pixel-art lettering for a label like "KOALA."

I'm building a tiny glyph dictionary for letters K, O, A, L to stamp onto the brass plaque, deciding "KOALA" is short enough to render cleanly. Moving on to the trunk, I'm designing a flared root sweep and then working out the eucalyptus bark coloring, using noise-driven cell painting to streak creams, greys, pale greens, and tans vertically to mimic peeling bark ribbons.

For the peeling bark itself, I'm planning thin tan card strips scattered across the trunk surface since each part counts against a 1000-part budget, so I'm aiming to keep the total around 500 parts by using single-texture cards for both bark strips and leaves. I'm also adding a dark knot/hole decal and a few small branch stubs as spikes on the trunk.

For the eucalyptus foliage, I'm designing a sickle-shaped leaf card texture in teal-green with a lighter midrib, then placing it on reddish-brown twig bundles with paired gumnuts (sphere-and-cone caps) near the branch tips where the koala appears to be eating. I'm generating hanging leaf frames along the twig path with randomized orientation and feeding them into the cards function to scatter foliage naturally.

Now I'm sketching the koala's skeleton: a spine chain from hips through chest and neck to the head and jaw, with ears, shoulders, elbows, wrists, fingers and thumbs on the arms, and hips, knees, ankles, and toes on the legs. For the body shape I'm thinking pear-like with an extra scaled sphere for the rounded rump, plus small pixel fur-tuft cards planned for the chest, cheeks, and ear fringes.

I'm working through fluffy pixel-art fur details around the cheeks and ear fringe using scattered triangle cards, tiny dark beady eyes with a highlight, cream-colored claw spikes on each digit, and dark charcoal paw and foot pads with opposable thumbs on the forepaws.

For the tail area, I'm thinking the koala should be tailless with a cream-white rump stub, maybe adding some brownish patch markings for realism. I'm considering whether to add extra details like a joey or a small bug on the branch, but leaning toward skipping the joey for simplicity while maybe tossing in a tiny ladybug accent.

Now I'm shifting to the head's joint placement and orientation, figuring out the neck-to-head attachment point and tilt angle so the koala's head leans slightly forward in a natural resting pose.

Axis alignment keeps grid consistency and hit detection simpler. For the skull's front face, I'm planning the fur texture using dithered sheet drawing rather than solid cell paint, layering eyes, pale muzzle, and white cheeks onto that pattern.

I'm sizing the head sheet so the texture stays grid-consistent with the body's colors, then adding a flat koala-style face with a muzzle box projecting forward, a dark nose sitting on top of the muzzle bridge, and a separate lower jaw box with a white chin below the upper jaw.

Working out skull proportions relative to the body—roughly 0.22x0.17x0.17 head size against a 0.30 hip width, keeping the head large and chunky. I'm placing the ears as angled discs at the sides, extruded with their facing plane tilted outward-forward.

Still computing the ear plane geometry...

Working out the ear's local axis vectors so the cream disc faces consistently forward regardless of mirroring...

Writing extrusion parameters...

For the ear, I'll go with radius 7 cells to keep the proportions chunky and koala-like relative to the head, using integer row half-widths for the outline. Then I'm defining the fur paint function, blending a base gradient value with noise to create texture across the body.

Still writing fur shading logic...

Now for the koala face itself, I need to plan out the distinctive features—grey brow, small black eyes, white cheeks, large black nose, pale muzzle and chin—laid out on a small front-face texture region using a skin layout helper for the head.

Still designing fur pixel details...

Now I'm working out the muzzle and nose geometry as separate protruding boxes in front of the head, positioning them centered on the face with the nose sitting atop the muzzle's upper half.

I'm figuring out the nose texture colors — a leathery black bulb with subtle grey highlights — and then setting up the lower jaw box with pale cream fur and a dark mouth gap, pivoted at the jaw joint for potential animation.

For positioning, I realize head-local direction words like forward/up are tied to the model's frame regardless of orientation, so I can use them directly without worrying about tilt. Now I'm moving on to placing the shoulder joints symmetrically on the chest and sizing the upper arms toward the elbow.

Working out hand placement on the branch, I'm checking the distance from shoulder to wrist against the combined upper-arm and forearm lengths, finding the arm is slightly too short for a straight reach, so I need to bend the elbow outward to make up the difference.

I'm sorting out which world axis corresponds to left versus right for the limb bend hints, settling on a convention where left uses +X, then positioning the hands so fingers wrap over the branch's outer face while thumbs hook underneath for a natural gripping pose.

To avoid overlapping hands along the branch, I'm staggering them at slightly different z-positions, and planning to compute the exact grip point by sampling the branch's path curve at those positions.

Now I'm working out the hand geometry: a palm box sitting on top of the branch with a few fingers curling forward and then down around the cylindrical surface, wrapping outward and downward in the cross-sectional plane to mimic a natural grip.

Let me reconsider the hand positioning: arms come from the shoulder forward with the palm facing inward toward the branch, fingers curling over the top and down the opposite side, positioning the left hand at the branch's left side and setting its orientation accordingly.

Working out finger and thumb arcs...

I'm checking the arm geometry from shoulder to wrist, measuring the reach distance and adjusting elbow bend so the limb hugs the branch realistically without overstretching, then applying similar grip placement logic to the hind feet.

Now I'm working through the hind legs straddling the branch, placing feet at mirrored x positions with toes curling over the top like the hands, but checking for collisions between the gripping feet and the rump or lower belly given their close z-coordinates.

I'm settling on hands and feet at slightly different heights along the branch's slope so they don't overlap with the belly, confirming the rump sphere sits cleanly on the branch top, and then working out hip-to-knee-to-ankle joint positions for the thighs and shins with proper lengths and angles.

Now I'm placing the foot pad relative to the branch center and tapering the thigh and shin radii, then laying out the spine chain from hips through spine2, chest, and neck as a sweep of connected points.

Skipping a tail since koalas don't have one. I'm defining the joint chains: a "spine" chain of hips/spine/chest spanning to the neck base, then a separate "neck" chain running to the head base, with the head attached as its own joint. For body shape, I'm planning to sweep a pear-like profile that's wider at the bottom near the hips.

For the sweep radii, I'm tapering the body thickness along the chain—wide at the hips (around .17) narrowing down to about .09 near the neck base, using separate x/y values for an elliptical cross-section rather than a perfect circle. The bottom cap sinks slightly below the branch surface so it reads as sitting naturally on it, and I'm keeping the neck short and stubby with its own thin joint for rigging purposes.

I'm adding fluffy chest and cheek details since koalas have that characteristic ruff. For the stand, I'm setting up the root joint at the origin with hips parented to it and the rest of the chain following naturally, with shoulders offset to the sides for the arms. Now I'm working out the trunk and seat branch geometry—plotting a curved path of points that rises and bends outward from the trunk around y=0.4 to form the seat the koala rests on, with radius tapering from thicker at the base to thinner near the top.

I'm adjusting the trunk's lean so its front face sits close to the koala's back without actually touching, shifting the path points slightly forward as it rises so the gap stays believable. I'm also planning two extra side branches jutting off the trunk near y~0.95, one angling left and up, the other right and up, each ending in leaf clusters, plus a small leafy twig near the seat branch's tip for added realism.

Now I'm designing a leafy twig helper that sweeps a thin branch and attaches card-shaped leaf clusters along it, orienting the leaf frames so they hang down like real eucalyptus foliage with some outward spread and randomized lean/spin for natural variety, then sketching a slender sickle-shaped pixel texture for each leaf.

Writing leaf pixel texture...

For gumnuts, I'll model them as small low-segment spheres with a cap, colored brownish-green, scattered a few per twig cluster.

Now for the trunk bark, I'm defining a color ramp from muted browns through greenish and pinkish tints, and using noise sampled across stretched coordinates to create streaky pixel patterns along the bark surface.

For the base, I'm darkening the lower portion to simulate a stringy root texture, and reusing the trunk's paint logic for branches. For the plinth, I'm considering horizontal wood plank tiling, possibly shaping it as a rounded octagon.

I'll scatter moss tufts, pebbles, and fallen leaves on the plinth using flat leaf cards leaned up and mirrored, with random orientation for the fallen leaves. I should also double-check tile grid uniformity for the plinth surface to keep texel scale consistent.

Now I'm designing a small pixel font for the plaque letters K, O, A, L using 3x5 glyphs, then laying out a 21x7 texture to spell "KOALA" with dark letters on a brass background.

For placement, I'm positioning the plaque flat on the plinth's top surface near the front, oriented so it reads correctly from the front-above viewing angle. Now I'm setting up the imports and builder utilities before writing the main scene construction code.

Still trimming imports and checking builder API signatures for parts, joints, and sweeps before I define the coordinate constants...

input.command: cd ~/tmp-archive/sonnet-100/koalaSonnet && grep -n "cards(\|stick(\|decal(\|slab(\|extrude(\|lathe(\|  sweep(\|  part(\|  surface(" src/builder.ts | head -30; ls src
